item.text: {"question_id":"2B.10","answer":"During 2023, Tshisekedi operated amid an inherited and externally entangled eastern conflict involving more than 100 armed groups, M23, regional intervention, and weak state capacity; the record therefore cannot attribute the adverse end state to him alone (BATCH-0012-R04-E001; BATCH-0010-E003; BATCH-0013-E014; BATCH-0027-E006; BATCH-0027-E007). He nevertheless exercised some relevant authority: he chaired planning with FARDC, MONUSCO, and the EAC force to implement ceasefire, withdrawal, disarmament, and cantonment provisions (BATCH-0021-E001); the Nairobi and Luanda processes produced ceasefire, monitoring, withdrawal, humanitarian-access, and P-DDRCS commitments (BATCH-0027-E010; BATCH-0027-E013); and a joint MONUSCO disengagement plan was signed, with intended civilian-protection, disarmament, security-sector, justice, and criminal-justice capacities (BATCH-0010-E007). These efforts had limited interim effects: the March ceasefire broadly held until early October, April ceasefire arrangements reduced hostilities for several months, and early-year M23 withdrawals enabled some road reopening and gradual returns (BATCH-0018-E002; BATCH-0027-E006; BATCH-0023-E010). UNJHRO also documented a 12% annual decline in recorded violations, including in conflict provinces, although incomplete reporting and changing conflict composition limit what that decline demonstrates (BATCH-0025-E009). The gains were not durable by period-end. The ceasefire broke down, M23 gained territory, late-year fighting displaced more than 450,000 people and raised national displacement to roughly 6.9 million, and M23’s occupation and attacks produced further mass displacement (BATCH-0027-E006; BATCH-0027-E007; BATCH-0013-E014; BATCH-0006-E002). The EAC mission ended after disagreements and without substantial progress, while government support for Wazalendo and FDLR alongside FARDC, private military contracting, and armed-drone acquisition increased risks of proxy abuse and regional escalation (BATCH-0011-E016; BATCH-0028-E016). Accountability and durable implementation were also weak: HRW reported no concrete domestic justice progress, unvetted integration of surrendered fighters, and continuing impunity, despite consultations and a stated cooperation request to the ICC (BATCH-0010-E015). Overall, Tshisekedi showed attributable diplomatic and institutional effort, with some short-term easing and formal peace architecture, but the evidence does not demonstrate that he left international relations more peaceful, stable, or lawful by the end of the 2023 period. The adverse end state is real but only partly attributable to him, given armed-group agency, alleged neighboring-state involvement, regional-force limitations, and inherited conflict conditions.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0012-R04-E001","BATCH-0021-E001","BATCH-0027-E010","BATCH-0027-E013","BATCH-0010-E007","BATCH-0018-E002","BATCH-0027-E006","BATCH-0023-E010","BATCH-0025-E009"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0010-E003","BATCH-0013-E014","BATCH-0006-E002","BATCH-0027-E007","BATCH-0011-E016","BATCH-0028-E016","BATCH-0010-E015"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The period ends amid active conflict, so the durability of the MONUSCO transition plan, P-DDRCS, ceasefire mechanisms, and other institutional arrangements cannot yet be established.","Most adverse outcomes involve multiple armed, regional, and external actors; the supplied evidence does not isolate Tshisekedi’s causal responsibility for battlefield developments, displacement, ceasefire breakdown, or ADF violence.","The documented decline in human-rights violations is incomplete and may reflect reporting conditions or changes in conflict composition; it is not a direct measure of lawful international relations.","Several peace and transition sources document plans, commitments, or intended capacities rather than verified implementation or durable settlement outcomes.","The supplied record is stronger on conflict outcomes and formal peace initiatives than on the ruler’s internal deliberation, enforcement of proxy controls, or personal accountability decisions."],"corrections_made":["Balanced the UNJHRO decline as relevant mixed evidence rather than minimizing it.","Added early-2023 ceasefire holding, limited returns, road reopening, and formal transition and justice-capacity planning.","Separated armed-group, neighboring-state, regional-force, and other external agency from direct presidential attribution.","Preserved the distinction between formal commitments and verified durable outcomes.","Added the supplied evidence on proxy support, accountability gaps, and weak justice implementation as qualifying evidence."],"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":["Reopen if evidence of Tshisekedi’s direct orders, enforcement decisions, or corrective actions concerning Wazalendo, FDLR, FARDC conduct, ceasefires, or justice accountability becomes available.","Reopen after later evidence can test whether the 2023 ceasefire, MONUSCO transition, P-DDRCS, and related institutions produced durable peace and lawful security outcomes.","Reopen if independently verified evidence clarifies the attribution of late-2023 M23 gains, displacement, or regional escalation."]}
